is_name_purposeful.instructions: Judge, in order: this unit's declared name, then its parameters, then its locals. A name fails when it is a bare generic word that could label anything (data, handler, util, temp), truncates its words into abbreviations a reader must decode (calc, proc, usr), names the mechanism instead of the purpose, or misleads.
criteria: Purposeful: every name states what its thing does or holds - a reader can tell each thing's purpose from the name alone, without opening the body.

Mostly purposeful: the names carry the unit's meaning overall, but at least one falls short - generic, truncated, mechanism-named, or misleading - so a reader must sometimes open the body to know what a thing is.
Names carry no meaning: the unit's names are habitually generic or opaque, so a reader must read the body for nearly everything the unit does or holds.

is_naming_convention_consistent.instructions: Do identifiers of the same kind in this unit follow a single casing convention?

criteria.true: Identifiers of the same kind follow one casing convention - functions and variables in camelCase, types and classes in PascalCase, module-level constants in SCREAMING_SNAKE - or whichever single form the surrounding code has already established for that kind.
criteria.false: Two different casing forms appear for the same kind within the change or module (getUserData beside fetch_user_data for two functions, OrderItem beside order_item for two types), forcing a reader to learn two shapes for one kind. Different kinds may use different conventions, and word choice or name quality are not casing failures.

is_greppable.instructions: Are the identifiers in this function searchable with terms a developer would use to find this code?

criteria.true: The code identifiers judged here are those in the function's declaration and body - its own name, its parameters, its locals, and the names it reads - and they are greppable: written out in full at every occurrence, never split into fragments or dynamically constructed from pieces, never renamed at a boundary, and specific enough that a search hit is genuinely a reference to this thing.
criteria.false: At least one identifier in the function cannot be found by a single search: it is split into fragments or dynamically constructed from pieces, renamed at a boundary so the same concept needs two search strings, or is a bare word (data, handler, util) whose hits are mostly noise. CLI flag spellings, help text, and log messages are user-facing interface, not code identifiers, and are outside this rule.

will_error_lose_cause.instructions: Does this function's error handling lose information about the original failure?

criteria.true: Error handling loses information: a caught error is swallowed, rethrown without its cause, or replaced by a message that drops the original failure detail.
criteria.false: Error handling preserves information: causes are chained, messages include the original failure detail, and nothing is swallowed silently.

is_cognitively_complex.instructions: How much EFFORT does a reader need to follow this code's logic - effort caused by structure the author chose, not by the problem itself? Ignore length alone: a long linear unit with one job reads as easy. Ignore inherent complexity: cases the data or the domain genuinely force are not this failure. Judge how hard the code's own structure makes it to read top-to-bottom.
criteria: Easy: the logic reads top-to-bottom. A single pass suffices. Any difficulty present is inherent to the problem, not to the structure.

Moderate: the reader must pause once or twice - hold a small amount of state across a few lines, or re-check an outer condition - but the structure is otherwise linear and the full flow is recoverable by re-reading one or two spots.

Hard: following the code requires actively reconstructing its flow - a stack of nested conditions to track, several unrelated concerns fused into one unit, state held across many lines, or an order that forces jumps instead of top-to-bottom reading. The structural difficulty could be removed without changing what the code does.

is_function_srp.instructions: Does this unit serve a single cohesive responsibility, every step serving one stated purpose?

criteria.true: The unit performs one cohesive responsibility: all its steps serve a single purpose its name and docblock state.
criteria.false: There is more than one reason for the unit to change: it mixes business logic, data validation, and side effects.
